Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2},$ where 

- ${C}_{1}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{1}(t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j$ for $t\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ and

- ${C}_{2}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{2}(t)=t\,i+\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region." :question/worked-solution "First, let $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ 

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and   

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented. 

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=i\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & =-{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-1}^{1}t\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t-0 \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{t}{2}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[\frac{\pi }{4}-0]-[-\frac{\pi }{4}-0] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cdfd2c93-cc42-5e18-b039-6099f904aa29"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-cdfd2c93-cc42-5e18-b039-6099f904aa29" :answer-field/id #uuid "cdfd2c93-cc42-5e18-b039-6099f904aa29" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-bbaa8abc-d95e-51ca-a4d1-7a1aa516b455" :answer-field/choices ["answer-94960e82-187d-589c-a1c2-ed096c94c497" "answer-6fe86c01-fa33-54c0-919e-aaad045de4dc" "answer-f46a71c6-0e54-5d62-9732-93eefd0150bf" "answer-bbaa8abc-d95e-51ca-a4d1-7a1aa516b455" "answer-91cc57eb-09e7-59eb-aa0f-280a8c492891"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-94960e82-187d-589c-a1c2-ed096c94c497" :answer/id #uuid "94960e82-187d-589c-a1c2-ed096c94c497" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6fe86c01-fa33-54c0-919e-aaad045de4dc" :answer/id #uuid "6fe86c01-fa33-54c0-919e-aaad045de4dc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f46a71c6-0e54-5d62-9732-93eefd0150bf" :answer/id #uuid "f46a71c6-0e54-5d62-9732-93eefd0150bf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5\pi }{2}-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bbaa8abc-d95e-51ca-a4d1-7a1aa516b455" :answer/id #uuid "bbaa8abc-d95e-51ca-a4d1-7a1aa516b455" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-91cc57eb-09e7-59eb-aa0f-280a8c492891" :answer/id #uuid "91cc57eb-09e7-59eb-aa0f-280a8c492891" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-fdacb1ae-ddf6-5106-9485-7c1e14bd18a9" :question/id #uuid "fdacb1ae-ddf6-5106-9485-7c1e14bd18a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-42297" :question/problem "![](images/35/35b8ad6fd40daf95ba4f77288321d6a570e2df2944d056b9445e9ba4e36f97b7.png)

"6ae04e3b-017d-534f-b76c-ac600584e435" :question/math-academy-id "q-126568" :question/problem "Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the functions $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)?$

I. $P(x,y)=-y-\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$

II. $P(x,y)=x$ and $Q(x,y)=y$

III. $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=6{y}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "According to Green's theorem, if 

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Pair I gives the required area. In this case,
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1+\operatorname{sin}⁡y$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

- Pair II does *not* give the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0\ne 1.
$$

- Pair III gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1557ad1a-a45b-592a-8609-24271802b200"] :db/ensure :question/problem "![](images/86/86772e27f0a3226a608a1188fd8f58b9a8956f5f02fdbc5f9c2d29e2cef2a54c.png)

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region enclosed by the curve 
$C$ parametrized as $r(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,j$ 
for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$" :question/worked-solution "First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i+12\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,dx & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\cdot (-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡2t(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-18{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =18{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =6({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0b42e264-51ff-5675-8ac9-a399601959a2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-6I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-1I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $V:$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c4360e51-0f64-590c-bba8-917045fffada"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id The function $f(x)$ is defined and differentiable on $[-2,5].$ The graph of $f'(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ is shown above, where the area of the region between the graph and the $x$-axis is $8.$ Find the minimum value of $f(x)$ on the interval $[-2,5]$ given that $f(-2)=4.$" :question/worked-solution "According to the candidates test, the minimum value of $f(x)$ on $[-2,5]$ must occur at a critical point or an endpoint of the interval.

**Step 1**: Find the critical points.

We see that $f'(x)$ is defined everywhere on $x \in (-2,5),$ and $f'(x) \neq 0$ on this interval. Therefore, the candidates are $x=-2,5.$

**Step 2**: Compute the value of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-2) & =4 \\ f(5) & =f(-2)+{\int }_{-2}^{5}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4-8 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Select the smallest value of $f$ from our candidates.

Comparing the values of $f$ found in step $2,$ we have

$$
f_{\text{min}} = \min\{4, -4\} = -4.
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is $f_{\text{min}} = -4,$ and the value of $x$ that minimizes $f(x)$ is $x_{\text{min}} = 5.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100862 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e74c85cc-5f64-54fa-a3ca-fa87e47bcbd2" "question-6cbda409-a223-57c5-93ac-3f78fe61c842" "question-4760d6e4-5155-5d78-b6d2-f55eb97036fb" "question-20a7e745-4621-5ebb-935e-e596b9f08fba"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100702 :question/problem "The function $f(x)$ is defined and differentiable on $[1,9].$ The graph of $f'(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ is shown below, where the areas of the regions between the graph and the $x$-axis are $3,$ $5,$ and $4$ respectively (from left to right). We see that $f'(x)$ is defined everywhere on $x \in (1,9),$ and $f'(x) = 0$ at $x=3$ and $x=6.$ Therefore, the candidates are $x=1,3,6,9.$

**Step 2**: Compute the values of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =5 \\ f(3) & =f(1)+{\int }_{1}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5+3 \\  & =8 \\ f(6) & =f(1)+{\int }_{1}^{6}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5+3-5 \\  & =3 \\ f(9) & =f(1)+{\int }_{1}^{9}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5+3-5+4 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Select the smallest value of $f$ from our candidates.

$$
f_{\text{min}} = \min\{5, 8, 3, 7\} = 3.

Let's understand how this process works by studying a specific example.

The graph of $y = f'(x),$ the *derivative* of $f(x),$ is shown in the picture below. 

![](images/2e/2ee1721d439ee0234b0f8a99ed0e4a56c63041e36919b00978267cf361a5322c.png)

The areas of the shaded regions are indicated on the diagram. Additionally, it is known that $f(-2)=5.$ Our goal is find the *minimum* value of $f(x)$ on the interval $x\in [-2,2].$

To find the minimum value of $f(x),$ we use the candidates test.

According to the candidates test, the minimum value of $f(x)$ on $[-2,2]$ must occur at a critical point or an endpoint of the interval. Therefore, we proceed as follows.

**Step 1**: Find the critical points.

We see that $f'(x)$ is defined everywhere on $x\in (-2,2),$ so there are no non-stationary critical points. Additionally, we see that $f'(x)=0$ at $x=1.$ Therefore, the candidates are 

$$
x=-2,\quad x=1,\quad x=2.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the value of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus.

- The value of $f(x)$ at the left endpoint is given:

$$
f(-2) = 5
$$

- To compute $f(1),$ we apply the fundamental theorem of calculus. Since the areas of the rectangle and middle triangle in our picture equal ${\color{red}{2}}$ and ${\color{red}{\dfrac12}},$ respectively, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =f(-2)+{\int }_{-2}^{1}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5-2-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we *subtracted* these areas since both lie *under* the $x$-axis.

- To compute $f(2),$ we apply the fundamental theorem of calculus once more. Using the fact that the area of the right triangle equals ${\color{blue}{\dfrac12}},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & =f(-2)+{\int }_{-2}^{2}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5-2-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Select the smallest value of $f$ from our candidates. 

Comparing the values of $f$ found in step $2,$ we have

$$
f_{\text{min}} = \min\left\lbrace 5, \dfrac52, 3 \right\rbrace = \dfrac52.
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is $f_{\text{min}}=\dfrac52,$ and the value of $x$ that minimizes $f(x)$ is $x_\text{min}=1.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101090 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192712 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f302fed8-a5b6-5ab4-978d-2dce7c91e287" "question-0272db1e-3587-51d4-ba80-cbc263d01f1e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-f302fed8-a5b6-5ab4-978d-2dce7c91e287" :question/id #uuid "f302fed8-a5b6-5ab4-978d-2dce7c91e287" :question/math-academy-id "q-149437" :question/problem "The table below gives the values of a positive, continuous function $f(x)$ over the closed interval $[0,12].$

- If $g(x)$ is strictly increasing, the right Riemann sum gives an *overestimate* of the area under the curve $y=g(x).$

- If $g(x)$ is strictly decreasing, the right Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the area under the curve $y=g(x).$

Let's now consider each statement in turn:

- Statement I is false. Since $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- Statement II is false. Differentiating $g(x)={x}^{3}\cdot f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{3})^{′}\cdot f(x)+{x}^{3}\cdot {f}^{′}(x) \\  & =3{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)+{x}^{3}\cdot {f}^{′}(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x)$ is positive and strictly increasing over the interval $(5,10),$ we have 

$$
3{x}^{2}>0,\,f(x)>0,\,{x}^{3}>0,\,{f}^{′}(x)>0.
$$

Hence, we obtain

$$
{g}^{′}(x)={{3{x}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{>0}\cdot {{f(x)}_{⏟}}_{>0}+{{{x}^{3}}_{⏟}}_{>0}\cdot {{{f}^{′}(x)}_{⏟}}_{>0}={{3{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)}_{⏟}}_{>0}+{{{x}^{3}\cdot {f}^{′}(x)}_{⏟}}_{>0}>0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since ${g}^{′}(x)>0,$ the function $g(x)$ is strictly increasing. Therefore, the right Riemann sum gives an *overestimate* of the area under the curve $y={x}^{3}\cdot f(x).$

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=-6x$ for $y\le 0,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$  represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at $(-3,0,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=-6x$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =-6x \\ {\rho }^{2} & =-6\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho +6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](images/df/df8a9da3b88f3b40d85005b156215f7fa7760257f284acf98ec186d5a2e3ab8d.png)

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-60daa8fe-705e-5990-9f0d-a1092f6eb497"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Determine the critical points of $f(x,y)=x{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}.$" :question/worked-solution "The critical points of a multivariable function $f$ are the points $a$ in the domain of $f$ such that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ or ${f}^{′}(a)$ does not exist, where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}.
$$

In this case, the domain of $f$ is ${R}^{2},$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(1-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2xy{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the first derivative of $f$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}(1-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} & -2xy{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the critical points, we need to find the points $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$ such that ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}$ or ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ does not exist. Note that, in our case, ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ exists everywhere, so we just need to find the points where ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}.$

Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we have the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(1-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}=0 \\ -2xy{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\ne 0$ for any point $(x,y)\in {R}^{2},$ we must have 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1-2{x}^{2}=0 \\ -2xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $x$ in the first equation, we get

$$
1-2{x}^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

 

Substituting these values into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-(\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})y=0\,⟹\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our system has two solutions, $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0)$ and $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0).$

In conclusion, $f$ has two critical points, $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0)$ and $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0).$ Note that since ${f}^{′}(x)={0}^{T}$ at these two points, they are also both stationary points." $$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}.
$$

In this case, the domain of $f$ is ${R}^{2},$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={y}^{2}-4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2xy+8.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the first derivative of $f$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4 & 2xy+8\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the critical points, we need to find the points $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$ such that ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}$ or ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ does not exist. Note that, in our case, ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ exists everywhere, so we just need to find the points where ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}.$

Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we have the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4=0 \\ 2xy+8=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $x$ in the second equation, we get

$$
2xy+8=0\,⟹\,x=-\frac{4}{y}.
$$

Now, solving for $y$ in the first equation, we get

$$
{y}^{2}-4=0\,⟹\,y=\pm 2.
$$

Substituting these values into $x=-\frac{4}{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=-2 & \,⟹\,x=-\frac{4}{(-2)}=2 \\ y=2 & \,⟹\,x=-\frac{4}{2}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our system has two solutions, $(2,-2)$ and $(-2,2).$

In conclusion, $f$ has two critical points, $(2,-2)$ and $(-2,2).$ Note that since ${f}^{′}(x)={0}^{T}$ at these two points, they are also both stationary points." :question/difficulty "Determine the stationary point of $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+4xy+{y}^{2}+4y.$" :question/worked-solution "The stationary points of a multivariable function $f$ are the points $a$ in the domain of $f$ such that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T},$ where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}.
$$

In tihs case, the domain of $f$ is ${R}^{2},$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =4x+4y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =4x+2y+4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first derivative of $f$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+4y & 4x+2y+4\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the stationary points, we need to find the points where ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}.$
Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we have the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x+4y=0 \\ 4x+2y+4=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $x$ in the first equation, we get

$$
4x+4y=0\,⟹\,x=-y.
$$

Then, substituting $x=-y$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(-y)+2y+4 & =0 \\ -4y+2y+4 & =0 \\ -2y & =-4 \\ y & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting this value into $x=-y,$ we obtain

$$
y=2\,⟹\,x=-2.
$$

Therefore, our system has one solution, $(-2,2).$

In conclusion, $f$ has one stationary point, $(-2,2).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a7580df7-3ea9-5eba-8784-550ab709f1c8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a7580df7-3ea9-5eba-8784-550ab709f1c8" :answer-field/id #uuid "a7580df7-3ea9-5eba-8784-550ab709f1c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1af52b2f-5397-5a81-abc1-978645b4d1a2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1af52b2f-5397-5a81-abc1-978645b4d1a2" "answer-89248e74-a748-5084-86b6-3604e1ebdb8d" "answer-878c880e-3b54-584e-b46c-b726a887844e" "answer-32a95250-bdf5-5705-8ecc-b001eba9f20b" "answer-7eca7f5a-6e66-5afe-a187-bb1fac895726"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1af52b2f-5397-5a81-abc1-978645b4d1a2" :answer/id #uuid "1af52b2f-5397-5a81-abc1-978645b4d1a2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-2,2)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-89248e74-a748-5084-86b6-3604e1ebdb8d" :answer/id #uuid "89248e74-a748-5084-86b6-3604e1ebdb8d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(0,4)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-878c880e-3b54-584e-b46c-b726a887844e" :answer/id #uuid "878c880e-3b54-584e-b46c-b726a887844e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(2,2)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-32a95250-bdf5-5705-8ecc-b001eba9f20b" :answer/id #uuid "32a95250-bdf5-5705-8ecc-b001eba9f20b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(4,0)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7eca7f5a-6e66-5afe-a187-bb1fac895726" :answer/id #uuid "7eca7f5a-6e66-5afe-a187-bb1fac895726" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "No stationary points" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-1640e015-4c92-5aff-b3e3-71cc75c19c43" :question/id #uuid "1640e015-4c92-5aff-b3e3-71cc75c19c43" :question/math-academy-id "q-105280" :question/problem "Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function 
$f(x,y)$ 
given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}) & -2y{e}^{x}\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}) & -2y{e}^{x}\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2y{e}^{x}.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2})=0 \\ -2y{e}^{x}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the second equation for $y,$ we get

$$
-2y{e}^{x}=0\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

Then, substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{0}^{2}) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x & =0 \\ x(x+2) & =0 \\ x & =-2,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $(0,0)$ and $(-2,0)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}))={e}^{x}({x}^{2}+4x-{y}^{2}+2)\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y{e}^{x})=-2y{e}^{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}))=-2y{e}^{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y{e}^{x})=-2{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({x}^{2}+4x-{y}^{2}+2) & -2y{e}^{x} \\ -2y{e}^{x} & -2{e}^{x}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get

$$
H(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))=2\cdot (-2)-{0}^{2}=-4<0,
$$

Therefore, $f(0,0)$ is a saddle point.

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(-2,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-2,0)=[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-2} & 0 \\ 0 & -2{e}^{-2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(-2,0),$ we get

$$
H(-2,0)=det({f}^{″}(-2,0))=(-2{e}^{-2})^{2}-{0}^{2}=4{e}^{-4}>0
$$

Finally, since $H(-2,0)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-2,0)=({f}^{″}(-2,0))_{11}=-2{e}^{-2}<0,$ the function $f$ has a local maximum at $(-2,0).$

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local maximum at $(-2,0).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125891 :tutorial/content "The **second partial derivatives test** helps to determine whether a stationary point of a function of two variables gives rise to a local maximum, a local minimum, or a saddle point.

Suppose that $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a}$ is a critical point of $f(\mathbf x),$ and let $H(\mathbf{a})$ denote the determinant of $\boldsymbol f''(x,y)$ evaluated at $\mathbf{a}$ (recall that $H(\mathbf a)$ is called the *Hessian determinant* of $f$ at $\mathbf a$).

The second partial derivative test states the following:

- If $H(\mathbf{a}) > 0,$ then:

- if $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(\mathbf{a}) < 0,$  then $f$ has a local maximum at $\mathbf{a},$ and

- if $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(\mathbf{a}) > 0,$  then $f$ has a local minimum at $\mathbf{a}.$

- If $H(\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $\mathbf{a}.$

- If $H(\mathbf{a}) = 0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive, and we need to classify the point using some other method.

As an example, consider the function $f (x, y) = 3 + 2x^2 - x y + y^2.$ Let's find the critical points of this function and then classify them using the second partial derivatives test.

We start by computing the partial derivatives:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 4x -y, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2y -x
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \mathbf{0}^T,$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x-y=0 \\ 2y-x=0,\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is $x=0, y=0.$ Hence, $(0,0)$ is the only stationary point.  

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-y)=4 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y-x)=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y-x)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get

$$
H(0,0) = \det(\boldsymbol f''(0,0)) = 4 \cdot 2 - (-1)^2 = 7 > 0.
$$

Finally, since $H(0,0) > 0$ and $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(0,0) = (\boldsymbol f''(0,0))_{11}= 4 >0,$ the function $f$ has a local minimum at $(0,0).$

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162110 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-af95ddae-1d2c-5a3d-9f8a-8a341d008cae"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162378 :question/problem "Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{50}∼N(5,{10}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $50$ from a normal population, calculate $P(4.8<\overset{―}{X}<5.2).$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.1\,$ | $\,0.5398\,$ | $\,0.5438\,$ | $\,0.5478\,$ | $\,0.5517\,$ | $\,0.5557\,$ |
| $\,0.2\,$ | $\,0.5793\,$ | $\,0.5832\,$ | $\,0.5871\,$ | $\,0.5910\,$ | $\,0.5948\,$ |

| $\,0.4\,$ | $\,0.6554\,$ | $\,0.6591\,$ | $\,0.6628\,$ | $\,0.6664\,$ | $\,0.6700\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(5,\frac{{10}^{2}}{50}) \\  & ∼N(5,2).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(4.8<\overset{―}{X}<5.2).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4.8<\overset{―}{X}<5.2) & =P(\frac{4.8-5}{\sqrt{2}}<Z<\frac{5.2-5}{\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =P(-0.14<Z<0.14) \\  & =Φ(0.14)-Φ(-0.14)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(0.14)=0.5557,
$$

and by the symmetry of the normal distribution,

$$
\begin{aligned}\,Φ(-0.14) & =1-Φ(0.14) \\  & =1-0.5557 \\  & =0.4443.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4.8<\overset{―}{X}<5.2) & =Φ(0.14)-Φ(-0.14) \\  & =0.5557-0.4443 \\  & =0.1114.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186159470 :answer-field/correct 17592186159473 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-af95ddae-1d2c-5a3d-9f8a-8a341d008cae" :question/id #uuid "af95ddae-1d2c-5a3d-9f8a-8a341d008cae" :question/math-academy-id "q-143298" :question/problem "Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{18}∼N(2,{6}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $18$ from a normal population, calculate $P(|\overset{―}{X}|<1.05).$

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(2,\frac{{6}^{2}}{18}) \\  & ∼N(2,2).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|<1.05).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<1.05) & =P(-1.05<\overset{―}{X}<1.05) \\  & =P(\frac{-1.05-2}{\sqrt{2}}<Z<\frac{1.05-2}{\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =P(-2.16<Z<-0.67) \\  & =Φ(-0.67)-Φ(-2.16)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.67) & =0.2514, \\ Φ(-2.16) & =0.0154.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<1.05) & =Φ(-0.67)-Φ(-2.16) \\  & =0.2514-0.0154 \\  & =0.2360.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4cf4ed49-e9a9-55e6-9767-0a26348a3bfb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=\pi .$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{-}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=\pi .$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}(\pi ) & ={lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{-}}f(x)=1 \\ {f}^{+}(\pi ) & ={lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{+}}f(x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
\frac{{f}^{-}(\pi )+{f}^{+}(\pi )}{2}=\frac{1+0}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164979 :answer-field/correct "answer-735db7a5-7bcb-5fa9-a24e-2f32aa107ab9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-735db7a5-7bcb-5fa9-a24e-2f32aa107ab9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-735db7a5-7bcb-5fa9-a24e-2f32aa107ab9" :answer/id #uuid "735db7a5-7bcb-5fa9-a24e-2f32aa107ab9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186375034 :question/problem "$$

We will go through each subinterval of $[-1,8]$ and check if the IVT guarantees a solution to the equation $f(x)=-2$ on this interval.

- On the subinterval $[-1,0],$ we have $f(-1)=-5$ and $f(0)=0.$ Since $-2\in [-5,0],$ the IVT *does * guarantee a solution to the equation $f(x)=-2$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[0,2],$ we have $f(0)=0$ and $f(2)=4.$ Since $-2\notin [0,4],$ the IVT does *not* guarantee a solution to the equation $f(x)=-2$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[2,4],$ we have $f(2)=4$ and $f(4)=-1.$ Since $-2\notin [-1,4],$ the IVT does *not* guarantee a solution to the equation $f(x)=-2$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[4,5],$ we have $f(4)=-1$ and $f(5)=-4.$ Since $-2\in [-4,-1],$ the IVT *does* guarantee a solution to the equation $f(x)=-2$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[5,8],$ we have $f(5)=-4$ and $f(8)=8.$ Since $-2\in [-4,8],$ the IVT *does* guarantee a solution to the equation $f(x)=-2$ on this subinterval.

The IVT guarantees solutions to $f(x)=-2$ on the subintervals $[-1,0],$ $[4,5],$ and $[5,8].$ Therefore, $f(x)=-2$ has at least three solutions." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate *If $f(x)$ is continuous on $\color{blue}[a,b],$ and $k$ is a number between $\color{red}{f(a)}$ and $\color{red}{f(b)}$ inclusively, then there exists a number $c \in \color{blue}{[a,b]}$ such that $f(c)=k.$*

The intuition behind the IVT is that if a function is continuous between two inputs, then between those two inputs, we must be able to draw the function without picking up our pen off the page, so the function must cover all values between the two corresponding outputs.

The IVT is often used to prove that some equation has a solution. For example, if we want to prove that there is a solution to $f(x)=3,$ and we know that $f(x)$ is a continuous function with $f({\color{blue}{1}})={\color{red}{2}}$ and $f({\color{blue}{6}})={\color{red}{6}},$ then the IVT tells us that there exists some solution $c \in \color{blue}{[1,6]}$ such that $f(c)=3.$

We can gain further intuition by visualizing the situation. First, let's plot what $y=f(x)$ *might* look like.

![](images/98/9896ea1c3d3d7c461e78ce4b4b232ce1f13f329468cd28b2d8e743132de093df.png)

For this particular $f(x)$ there is one solution to $f(x)=3$, which is $x\approx 2.$ Note that our solution lies inside the interval $\color{blue}[1,6].$

Now let's consider another *possible* $f(x).$

![](images/de/dea5683d5b18bccf9623fb6a107e8ef818ddd1cef4adbef08be471869791ec27.png)

This time, there are three solutions to $f(x)=3$ which lie in the interval $\color{blue}[1,6].$ 

We can keep changing our $f(x),$ but no matter how we draw it, we will always have some solution to $f(x)=3$ which lies in the interval $\color{blue}[1,6].$

![](images/4d/4d4aaec84baff10a48f715eeae7e06af21beccd29b38c42b3283032ef0726fec.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135023 :tutorial/content "Consider the function $f(x)$ given below.
![](images/0d/0d18168108342ef8232063b58e46ef88cdff9fe54aa730dca872bc9755a42995.svg)
Can we apply the intermediate value theorem to $f(x)$ on the interval $[1,4]?$

Remember, the intermediate value theorem assumes that the function is continuous. Here, the function $f(x)$ not continuous on $[1,4].$ So, we cannot apply the intermediate value theorem.

If we plot the function, we can get an idea of why the intermediate value theorem cannot be applied.

![](images/9b/9b9543ec11b350cea4ca18e24a8db6ae8f72ffc38e64f973f9af2f83f1226400.png)

The graph shows that, for example, the equation $f(x)=1.5$ has no solution on $[1,4]$ despite the fact that $1.5$ lies between $f(1)=4$ and $f(4)=0.$
So, the intermediate value theorem does not hold.

**Watch out!** The interval on which we apply the intermediate value theorem must *always* be closed. For example, we can't apply the theorem on an interval like $[1,3).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134019 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{2}{9}$ | $\frac{1}{27}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{27}$ | $\frac{7}{27}$ | $\frac{1}{9}$ |

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=0]$ given that $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{Y|0}=2.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ let's first find the marginal distribution for $X,$ corresponding to the row totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ | ${f}_{X}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{2}{9}$ | $\frac{1}{27}$ | $\frac{16}{27}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{27}$ | $\frac{7}{27}$ | $\frac{1}{9}$ | $\frac{11}{27}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x$ is

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding row total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x:$

| ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{9}{16}$ | $\frac{3}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{16}$ | $1$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{11}$ | $\frac{7}{11}$ | $\frac{3}{11}$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=0] & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,0)]-{\mu }_{Y|0}^{2} \\  & =[{0}^{2}\cdot \frac{9}{16}+{4}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{8}+{8}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{16}]-{2}^{2} \\  & =0+6+4-4 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8e701f23-45b5-584b-9ff7-052c5c629f38"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8e701f23-45b5-584b-9ff7-052c5c629f38" :answer-field/id #uuid "8e701f23-45b5-584b-9ff7-052c5c629f38" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e3c50614-2143-5835-91a2-26951415d4a3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e3a0e51e-a2b2-5d25-84bb-27f6878f5ff2" "answer-e38c50ad-e0fc-52f2-b45a-0aed3bf8753b" "answer-e3c50614-2143-5835-91a2-26951415d4a3" "answer-3ec68043-b866-5e5b-8bb7-32d1408e60c0" "answer-c5e9e267-a7b8-546e-8ca5-7597e4f9d784"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e3a0e51e-a2b2-5d25-84bb-27f6878f5ff2" :answer/id #uuid "e3a0e51e-a2b2-5d25-84bb-27f6878f5ff2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e38c50ad-e0fc-52f2-b45a-0aed3bf8753b" :answer/id #uuid "e38c50ad-e0fc-52f2-b45a-0aed3bf8753b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e3c50614-2143-5835-91a2-26951415d4a3" :answer/id #uuid "e3c50614-2143-5835-91a2-26951415d4a3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3ec68043-b866-5e5b-8bb7-32d1408e60c0" :answer/id #uuid "3ec68043-b866-5e5b-8bb7-32d1408e60c0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c5e9e267-a7b8-546e-8ca5-7597e4f9d784" :answer/id #uuid "c5e9e267-a7b8-546e-8ca5-7597e4f9d784" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186188687 :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=2]$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{X|2}=5.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y,$ corresponding to the column totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |
| $X=9$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{3}{16}$ | $\frac{1}{16}$ |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $\frac{3}{8}$ | $\frac{5}{16}$ | $\frac{5}{16}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y:$

| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ | $\frac{2}{5}$ | $\frac{4}{5}$ |
| $X=9$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{3}{5}$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=2] & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)]-{\mu }_{X|2}^{2} \\  & =[{3}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}+{9}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}]-{5}^{2} \\  & =6+27-25 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-798593a5-cfe0-5f7d-84fa-43e7795c761a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-798593a5-cfe0-5f7d-84fa-43e7795c761a" :answer-field/id #uuid "798593a5-cfe0-5f7d-84fa-43e7795c761a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b3aef80f-ba63-5a2a-892f-31618b540913" :answer-field/choices ["answer-82fe3a83-b24a-5a3c-bffb-cf8e5344fd6a" "answer-66d1570e-0fc2-5b26-944e-0848dd40f138" "answer-9f3745f3-2e12-5887-955e-9fd687c8f6c3" "answer-b3aef80f-ba63-5a2a-892f-31618b540913" "answer-7e4bbbd8-2767-5014-b1ea-d2f03b69e408"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-82fe3a83-b24a-5a3c-bffb-cf8e5344fd6a" :answer/id #uuid "82fe3a83-b24a-5a3c-bffb-cf8e5344fd6a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-66d1570e-0fc2-5b26-944e-0848dd40f138" :answer/id #uuid "66d1570e-0fc2-5b26-944e-0848dd40f138" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9f3745f3-2e12-5887-955e-9fd687c8f6c3" :answer/id #uuid "9f3745f3-2e12-5887-955e-9fd687c8f6c3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b3aef80f-ba63-5a2a-892f-31618b540913" :answer/id #uuid "b3aef80f-ba63-5a2a-892f-31618b540913" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7e4bbbd8-2767-5014-b1ea-d2f03b69e408" :answer/id #uuid "7e4bbbd8-2767-5014-b1ea-d2f03b69e408" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-fa585366-16bd-5221-b5b1-a80000ac4783" :question/id #uuid "fa585366-16bd-5221-b5b1-a80000ac4783" :question/math-academy-id "q-146282" :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ |

The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero, while an inequality specifies a range of values.

Consider a simple absolute value inequality, as follows:

$$
|x| < 7
$$

This inequality specifies every number $x$ that is less than a distance of $7$ from $0$. So, it represents the same thing as the following compound inequality:

$$
-7 < x < 7
$$

To solve an absolute value inequality, we first convert it to a compound inequality to remove the absolute value. Then, we can solve the compound inequality using the usual methods.

To illustrate, let's solve the following inequality:

$$
|2x+3| \leq 5
$$

First, we interpret the inequality: the inequality specifies every number $2x+3$ whose distance from zero is less than or equal to $5.$ So, it represents the same thing as the following compound inequality:

$$
-5 \leq 2x+3 \leq 5
$$

Now, we can solve the compound inequality using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\le 2x+3\le 5 \\ -8\le 2x\le 2 \\ -4\le x\le 1\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186070027 :tutorial/content "We take a similar approach for absolute value inequalities involving the "greater than" symbol. To illustrate, consider the following absolute value inequality:

|x| \geq 6

To solve this absolute value inequality, we convert it into a compound inequality to remove the absolute value. The inequality specifies every number $x$ whose distance from zero is greater than or equal to $6.$ This corresponds to the following compound inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & \le -6 & \text{or} &  & x & \ge 6\end{aligned}
$$

We use the word "or" instead of "and" since only one of the inequalities $x\leq-6$ or $x\geq 6$ needs to be true for $|x| \geq 6$ to be true." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068978 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110630 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c3360eb5-04da-59fb-81da-119f0aeb047a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-c3360eb5-04da-59fb-81da-119f0aeb047a" :question/id #uuid "c3360eb5-04da-59fb-81da-119f0aeb047a" :question/math-academy-id "q-142529" :question/problem "![](images/96/96a76584c5ddbcc39d221334803c6791cb3b459178e70c310e4eca54a4e85462.png)

The angles $∠ODC$ and $∠FAO$ are interior to the parallel line segments and are on opposite sides of the transversal. So, they are alternate interior angles and consequently, they have the same measure.

In step 4, we found that $m∠ODC=5{x}^{∘}.$

Setting the measures of $∠ODC$ and $∠FAO$ equal to each other, we have an equation that we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠ODC & =m∠FAO \\ 5{x}^{∘} & =(3x+18)^{∘} \\ 5x & =3x+18 \\ 2x & =18 \\ x & =9\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠FAO & =(3x+18)^{∘} \\  & =(3\cdot 9+18)^{∘} \\  & ={45}^{∘} \\ m∠AOE & =(185-5x)^{∘} \\  & =(185-5\cdot 9)^{∘} \\  & ={140}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-y & -x\end{aligned}]$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-y & -x\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-x.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-y)=6x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-x)=-1 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-y)=-1\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}6x & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186155667 :answer-field/correct "answer-7cfd7658-f969-5d24-b54b-e78400ec350a" :answer-field/choices "Find ${f}^{″}(1,\pi )$ for the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y & {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y & 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & -{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(1,\pi ).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,\pi )=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dc17abaf-f11c-5b72-9671-ca1fd6cb7d81"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Find ${f}^{″}(0,-\frac{\pi }{2})$ for the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y).$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y) & -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y))=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y))=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y) \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y))=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y))=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y) \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(0,-\frac{\pi }{2}).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,-\frac{\pi }{2})=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a8dc6b69-1ae0-561f-a21b-1f490d47e054"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(0,0).$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & {e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)={e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$

$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(0,0)=(-1)\cdot 1-{0}^{2}=-1.

 since $x = 30$ corresponds to $30 \cdot 1\,000 = 30\,000$ copies of the newspaper.

If the textile center sells between $100$ and $900$ meters of fabric daily, how many meters of fabric must the textile center sell to maximize its revenue?" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & =x\cdot p(x) \\  & =x({x}^{2}-15x+48+\frac{78}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}+48x+78.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we note that the permitted domain is $1 \leq x \leq 9,$ since $x = 1$ corresponds to $1 \cdot 100 = 100$ and $x = 9$ corresponds to $9 \cdot 100 = 900.$ Therefore, $x=1$ and $x=9$ are both candidates for the global maxima of $R(x).$

We need to find the critical points of $R(x)$ for $1 <         x <         9.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$

$$

and solving $R'(x)=0$ gives the following critical points:

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-30x+48 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-10x+16 & =0 \\ (x-2)(x-8) & =0\end{aligned}

So, the critical points are $x=2$ and $x=8.$

Our candidates are $x=1,2, 8$ and $9.$ Computing $R(x)$ at each of these values, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}R(1) & =(1)^{3}-15(1)^{2}+48(1)+78=112 \\ R(2) & =(2)^{3}-15(2)^{2}+48(2)+78=122\,✓ \\ R(8) & =(8)^{3}-15(8)^{2}+48(8)+78=14 \\ R(9) & =(9)^{3}-15(9)^{2}+48(9)+78=24\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to maximize its revenue, the textile center should sell $2 \cdot 100 = 200$ meters of fabric." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101019 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-896ab313-4af7-5cfc-9d60-946032fe5a62" "question-de3d69db-3561-564d-a214-9ac683352f20" "question-a7b5b31e-6d04-57eb-9051-cd4496c07c09"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100660 :question/worked-solution "First, note that for selling $x$ units of the product per month, the company has a monthly revenue (income) of $R(x)=180\cdot x=180 x$ dollars.

{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Since $x$ represents the price of a single course and since the CFO estimates that the course price should be between $$1$ and $$7,$  the permitted domain for $x$ is given by

$$

$$

Since the second derivative is negative at $x=2,$ the point $x=2$ is indeed a local maximum of $P(x).$

First, note that if there are $x$ hundreds of *unsold* cups of coffee, the coffee shop sells $(5-x)$ hundreds of cups of coffee, and the price per cup is $(3+2x)$ dollars. So, the total revenue (in hundreds of dollars) is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & ={{(5-x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{sold cups of coffee}}\times \,\,\,{{(3+2x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{price per cup}} \\  & =15+10x-3x-2{x}^{2} \\  & =15+7x-2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, for selling $(5-x)$ hundreds of cups of coffee, the coffee shop has a cost (in hundreds of dollars) of 

$$
\begin{aligned}C(x) & =0.4(5-x) \\  & =2-0.4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the profit function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\ P(x) & =(15+7x-2{x}^{2})-(2-0.4x) \\  & =13+7.4x-2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We note that the permitted domain is $0\le x\le 5.$ 

We need to find the critical points of $P(x)$ for $0<x<5.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=7.4-4x,
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 7.4-4x & =0 \\ 4x & =7.4 \\ x & =1.85\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $x=1.85$ lies in the interval $0<x<5.$ All that's left now is to confirm that $x=1.85$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:

$$
{P}^{″}(x)=-4<0
$$

Since the second derivative is negative, the point $x=1.85$ is indeed a local maximum of $P(x).$ And since $P(x)$ is quadratic, we conclude that $x=1.85$ is a global maximum of $P(x).$ 

Therefore, we conclude that the coffee shop will have a maximum profit level when there are $185$ unsold cups of coffee.  

We know that the price per cup is $(3+2x)$ dollars. If there are $1.85$ hundreds of unsold cups of coffee, then the price per cup is

$$

$$

- Revenue: This is the total amount of money (in dollars) that a company gains after selling $x$ units of product.

- Cost: This is the total amount of money (in dollars) that a company spends to create $x$ units of product.

- Profit. The difference between revenue and cost. It represents the amount of *additional* money that the business has earned after paying its costs.

Businesses often strive to maximize revenue and profit. They also often seek to minimize cost. We can solve these problems using the second derivative or the candidates test. Let's find out how." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101994 :tutorial/content "Recall that the price function $p(x)$ gives the *price per unit* at which a company sells $x$ units of a good. 

The revenue function $R(x)$ associated with a price function $p(x)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & =(\text{number of units})\cdot (\text{price per unit}) \\  & =x\cdot p(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Also, recall that the cost function $C(x)$ associated with producing $x$ units of a good can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C(x) & =(\text{fixed cost})+(\text{number of units})\cdot (\text{cost per unit}) \\  & =(\text{fixed cost})+x\cdot (\text{cost per unit})\end{aligned}
$$

The quantity $x\cdot (\textrm{cost per unit})$ is sometimes called the **variable cost** since it is the part of the cost function $C(x)$ that is dependent on the number of units $x$ produced by the company. 

Finally, if we know the revenue function $R(x)$ and the cost function $C(x),$ then the profit function $P(x)$ is given by

$$
P(x) = R(x) - C(x).
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101072 :activity/expected-seconds 1500.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101902 :step/math-academy-id 644177 :db/ensure are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$" :question/worked-solution "The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1\end{aligned}]+(-2)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1\end{aligned}]+(-2)\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1\end{aligned}]+(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((3)\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}10 & -10 \\ -10 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b4cd93bf-3a8c-5f18-b352-8eff8b26fc90"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{13}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$

$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$" :question/worked-solution "If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-29dc167c-c1ad-5d54-8910-071c51c74e87"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).

- ${a}_{n},$ $n\ge 1,$ for the cosine coefficients, and

$$

customers per month." :question/worked-solution "First, we note that June $1$st corresponds to $t=1.$

We use the forward difference approximation formula

$$
{q}^{′}(t)≈\frac{q(t+h)-q(t)}{h}
$$

at the point $t=1.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible. In this case, we choose $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}^{′}(1) & ≈\frac{q(1+1)-q(1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{q(2)-q(1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{120-59}{1} \\  & =61.\end{aligned}
$$

So, using a forward difference approximation, the rate of change in the number of customers on June $1$st is approximately $61$ customers per month." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cf8bd0d4-e2df-5b96-ba24-b2e56674f0f8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-cf8bd0d4-e2df-5b96-ba24-b2e56674f0f8" :answer-field/id #uuid "cf8bd0d4-e2df-5b96-ba24-b2e56674f0f8" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-876c3c8e-19f9-56b2-a451-3c2578ba7af7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-876c3c8e-19f9-56b2-a451-3c2578ba7af7"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-876c3c8e-19f9-56b2-a451-3c2578ba7af7" :answer/id #uuid "876c3c8e-19f9-56b2-a451-3c2578ba7af7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "61" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092391 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7a6777e5-075d-540c-87f4-265fdb022242"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-7a6777e5-075d-540c-87f4-265fdb022242" :question/id #uuid "7a6777e5-075d-540c-87f4-265fdb022242" :question/math-academy-id "q-166363" :question/problem "From the given data, the best backward difference approximation for the rate at which the number of customers was changing on June $1$st is{{field-1}}
customers per month." :question/worked-solution "Again, we use the fact that June $1$st corresponds to $t=1.$

We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{q}^{′}(t)≈\frac{q(t)-q(t-h)}{h}
$$

at the point $t=1.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible. In this case, we choose $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}^{′}(1) & ≈\frac{q(1)-q(1-1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{q(1)-q(0)}{1} \\  & =\frac{59-0}{1} \\  & =59.\end{aligned}
$$

So, using a backward difference approximation, the rate of change in the number of customers on June $1$st is approximately $59$ customers per month." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-74caf0bf-cacd-5f28-aa72-d801b776ea5f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-74caf0bf-cacd-5f28-aa72-d801b776ea5f" :answer-field/id #uuid "74caf0bf-cacd-5f28-aa72-d801b776ea5f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-9593a22e-5aa8-5e2e-b0d9-870be17ad1c0" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9593a22e-5aa8-5e2e-b0d9-870be17ad1c0"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9593a22e-5aa8-5e2e-b0d9-870be17ad1c0" :answer/id #uuid "9593a22e-5aa8-5e2e-b0d9-870be17ad1c0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "59" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092181 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ae9e49ed-eef5-5e75-8ccc-b6af327fb845"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-ae9e49ed-eef5-5e75-8ccc-b6af327fb845" :question/id #uuid "ae9e49ed-eef5-5e75-8ccc-b6af327fb845" :question/math-academy-id "q-166364" :question/problem "Using a trapezoidal sum with two equal subintervals, ${\int }_{0}^{4}q(t)\,\text{d}t≈${{field-1}}
." :question/worked-solution "The general formula for the trapezoidal rule states that

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}q(t)\,\text{d}t≈\frac{1}{2}[q(a)+2(q({t}_{1})+q({t}_{2})+…+q({t}_{n-1}))+q(b)]Δt,
$$

where $n$ is the number of trapezoids and $Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}$ is the step size.

Here, we have the following values:

* The number of trapezoids is $n=2.$

* The corresponding interval is $[0,4],$ so we have $a=0$ and $b=4.$

* The step size is given by

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{4-0}{2}=2.
$$

Using the above values, the general formula becomes

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}q(t)\,\text{d}t≈\frac{1}{2}[q(0)+2q(2)+q(4)]\cdot 2.
$$

Substituting the appropriate numbers into the above expression gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}q(t)\,\text{d}t & ≈\frac{1}{2}[0+2(120)+108]\cdot 2 \\  & =240+108 \\  & =348.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dff10b37-1425-5f08-9969-ac5f0106b371"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-dff10b37-1425-5f08-9969-ac5f0106b371" :answer-field/id #uuid "dff10b37-1425-5f08-9969-ac5f0106b371" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-32acdae7-2eaa-5d7b-bea5-1d4a19711cdc" :answer-field/choices ["answer-32acdae7-2eaa-5d7b-bea5-1d4a19711cdc"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-32acdae7-2eaa-5d7b-bea5-1d4a19711cdc" :answer/id #uuid "32acdae7-2eaa-5d7b-bea5-1d4a19711cdc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "348" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064267 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6b1c7ad5-e07c-5b25-9e08-a2e2aa0ac237"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-6b1c7ad5-e07c-5b25-9e08-a2e2aa0ac237" :question/id #uuid "6b1c7ad5-e07c-5b25-9e08-a2e2aa0ac237" :question/math-academy-id "q-166365" :question/problem "Use your answer to part 3 to approximate the average number of customers at the campsite during the first $4$ months.

." :question/worked-solution "The average value of a continuous function $q(t)$ on a closed interval $[a,b]$ is given by

$$
{q}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}q(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We have that

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
{q}_{\text{ave}}≈\frac{348}{4-0}=87.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5847b751-f98d-563e-aaf4-cc2c04b1208d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5847b751-f98d-563e-aaf4-cc2c04b1208d" :answer-field/id #uuid "5847b751-f98d-563e-aaf4-cc2c04b1208d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-a73ce7dc-ebea-528a-9250-92701e8d78cb" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a73ce7dc-ebea-528a-9250-92701e8d78cb"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a73ce7dc-ebea-528a-9250-92701e8d78cb" :answer/id #uuid "a73ce7dc-ebea-528a-9250-92701e8d78cb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "87" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064273 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9de46d9e-0321-5243-8082-f7e3f4b58ad3"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-9de46d9e-0321-5243-8082-f7e3f4b58ad3" :question/id #uuid "9de46d9e-0321-5243-8082-f7e3f4b58ad3" :question/math-academy-id "q-166366" :question/problem "For $0\le t\le 8,$ the equation ${q}^{′}(t)=0$ has at least{{field-1}}
solution(s)." :question/worked-solution "The solutions to ${q}^{′}(t)=0$ correspond to the stationary points of the graph of $q(t).$

:answer-field/choices 17592186133288] [:db/retract 17592186133284 :answer-field/choices 17592186133289] {:db/id 17592186134541 :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|x/2|}}{4},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/2}}{2},\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/2}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/2}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133284 :answer-field/correct "answer-b905210f-a059-572c-8e25-2b36e139ca53" :answer-field/choices
