inequalities** combine two basic concepts: absolute value and inequality. The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero, while an inequality specifies a range of values.

Consider a simple absolute value inequality, as follows:

$$
|x| < 7
$$

This inequality specifies every number $x$ that is less than a distance of $7$ from $0$. So, it represents the same thing as the following compound inequality:

$$
-7 < x < 7
$$

To solve an absolute value inequality, we first convert it to a compound inequality to remove the absolute value. Then, we can solve the compound inequality using the usual methods.

To illustrate, let's solve the following inequality:

$$
|2x+3| \leq 5
$$

First, we interpret the inequality: the inequality specifies every number $2x+3$ whose distance from zero is less than or equal to $5.$ So, it represents the same thing as the following compound inequality:

$$
-5 \leq 2x+3 \leq 5
$$

Now, we can solve the compound inequality using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\le 2x+3\le 5 \\ -8\le 2x\le 2 \\ -4\le x\le 1\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186070027 :tutorial/content "We take a similar approach for absolute value inequalities involving the "greater than" symbol. To illustrate, consider the following absolute value inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & \le -6 & \text{or} &  & x & \ge 6\end{aligned}
$$

given that
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-y & -x\end{aligned}]$"] [17592186157791 :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-y & -x\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-x.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-y)=6x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-x)=-1 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-y)=-1\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}6x & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186157791 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-42ad8ac2-0cae-5d02-b554-16bcbaa98c5d" :answer/id #uuid "42ad8ac2-0cae-5d02-b554-16bcbaa98c5d"] $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$"] ["question-b2d69fc5-a88d-5940-a2a9-d7cc001b13e7" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y & {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y & 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & -{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(1,\pi ).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,\pi )=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b2d69fc5-a88d-5940-a2a9-d7cc001b13e7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-dc17abaf-f11c-5b72-9671-ca1fd6cb7d81" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Find ${f}^{″}(0,-\frac{\pi }{2})$ for the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y).$"] ["question-46310383-5e9b-5711-9143-446211dee40a" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y) & -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y))=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y))=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y) \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y))=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y))=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y) \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(0,-\frac{\pi }{2}).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,-\frac{\pi }{2})=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-46310383-5e9b-5711-9143-446211dee40a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-a8dc6b69-1ae0-561f-a21b-1f490d47e054" :answer-field/id #uuid {f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y & -{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

["question-223797a4-3fdc-5efb-a9f2-b733398cd415" :question/math-academy-id "q-80946"] ["question-223797a4-3fdc-5efb-a9f2-b733398cd415" :question/problem "Given that 
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & {e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}],$ 
evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(0,0).$"] ["question-223797a4-3fdc-5efb-a9f2-b733398cd415" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & {e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)={e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & -{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ -{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & {e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(0,0)=(-1)\cdot 1-{0}^{2}=-1.
$$"] ["question-223797a4-3fdc-5efb-a9f2-b733398cd415" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e7c15a59-5adc-5127-8074-bf8ca6a5dc2b" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "A school is organizing a trip to a theme park. The trip is offered to at least $12$ kids, and it can be attended by at most $20$ kids. The cost of each ticket is $$80$ if there are exactly $12$ kids. If there are more than $12$ kids, the price per ticket drops by $$4$ for each kid in excess of $12.$ Every kid pays the same amount for going on the trip.

How many kids must go on the trip for the theme park to maximize its revenue?"] ["question-83c84e0b-efbe-5ed1-89f6-e89dc6ca66e5" :question/worked-solution "First, note that if there are $12+x$ kids, then the price per ticket is $80-4x.$ So, the total revenue is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & ={{(12+x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{number of kids}}\times \,\,\,\,\,\,{{(80-4x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{price per ticket}} \\  & =(12+x)(80-4x) \\  & =960-48x+80x-4{x}^{2} \\  & =960+32x-4{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since there can only be between $12$ and $20$ kids, the permitted domain for $x$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & \le x+12\le 20 \\ 0 & \le x\le 8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=0$ and $x=8$ are both candidates for the global maxima of $R(x).$

We need to find the critical points of $R(x)$ for $0<x<8.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{R}^{′}(x)=32-8x,
$$

and solving ${R}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 32-8x & =0 \\ 8x & =32 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $x=4$ lies in the interval $0<x<8.$ All that's left now is to confirm that $x=4$ does indeed give a maximum value of $R(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:

$$
{R}^{″}(x)=-8<0
$$

Since the second derivative is negative, the point $x=4$ is indeed a local maximum of $R(x).$ And since $R(x)$ is quadratic, we conclude that $x=4$ is a global maximum of $R(x).$ 

Therefore, the theme park should admit $12+4=16$ kids to maximize its revenue."] ["question-83c84e0b-efbe-5ed1-89f6-e89dc6ca66e5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] $$
p(x)={x}^{2}-15x+63+\frac{11}{x}.
$$

If the store sells between $1$ and $6$ units of the product each day, how many units should the store sell to maximize its revenue?"] ["question-13ee04f2-9803-50aa-b0c0-1f54d4ebdeb4" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

First, note that for selling $x$ units in total, the total revenue $R(x)$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & =x\cdot p(x) \\  & =x({x}^{2}-15x+63+\frac{11}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}+63x+11.\end{aligned}

We need to find the critical points of $R(x)$ for $1<x<6.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{R}^{′}(x)=3{x}^{2}-30x+63,
$$

and solving ${R}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical points:

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-30x+63 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-10x+21 & =0 \\ (x-3)(x-7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the critical points are $x=3$ and $x=7.$ However, the value $x=7$ is not in the permitted domain, so the only new candidate is $x=3.$

Our candidates are $x=1,3$ and $6.$ Computing $R(x)$ at each of these values, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}R(1) & =(1)^{3}-15(1)^{2}+63(1)+11=60 \\ R(3) & =(3)^{3}-15(3)^{2}+63(3)+11=92\,✓ \\ R(6) & =(6)^{3}-15(6)^{2}+63(6)+11=65\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to maximize its revenue, the auto parts store should sell $3$ units."] ["question-13ee04f2-9803-50aa-b0c0-1f54d4ebdeb4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] :question/problem "A clothes store sells $x$ hundreds of pants at a price $p(x),$  in dollars, given by

$$
p(x)=200+40x-\frac{10}{3}{x}^{2}.
$$

If the store sells between $500$ and $1\,000$ pants per month, how many pants should it sell monthly to maximize its revenue?"] ["question-397e9b41-cb22-58e3-8777-87698586bfce" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

First, note that for selling $x$ pants, the total revenue $R(x)$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & =x\cdot p(x) \\  & =x(200+40x-\frac{10}{3}{x}^{2}) \\  & =200x+40{x}^{2}-\frac{10}{3}{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The permitted domain is $5\le x\le 10,$  since $x=5$  corresponds to $5\cdot 100=500$  and $x=10$ corresponds to $10\cdot 100=1\,000.$  Therefore, $x=5$ and $x=10$ are both candidates for the global maxima of $R(x).$

We need to find the critical points of $R(x)$ for $5<x<10.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{R}^{′}(x)=200+80x-10{x}^{2},
$$

and solving ${R}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical points:

$$

"a7b5b31e-6d04-57eb-9051-cd4496c07c09"] ["question-a7b5b31e-6d04-57eb-9051-cd4496c07c09" :question/math-academy-id "q-347264"] ["question-a7b5b31e-6d04-57eb-9051-cd4496c07c09" :question/problem "A factory spends  $C(x)=0.002375{x}^{2}+0.3x+1\,000$ dollars to manufacture $x$ units of a certain product. The factory sells the product for $30-\frac{x}{100}$ dollars per unit. Given that the factory can produce at most $2\,000$ units per year, how many units should the factory produce per year to maximize its annual profit?

The optimal number of production is
{{field-1}}."] ["question-a7b5b31e-6d04-57eb-9051-cd4496c07c09" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

First, note that for selling $x$ units of the product per year, the factory has an annual revenue (income) of $R(x)=(30-\frac{x}{100})\cdot x=30x-0.01{x}^{2}$ dollars.

Therefore, the profit function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\  & =30x-0.01{x}^{2}-(0.002375{x}^{2}+0.3x+1\,000) \\  & =-1\,000+29.7x-0.012375{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We note that the permitted domain is $0\le x\le 2\,000.$

We need to find the critical points of $P(x)$ for $0<x<2\,000.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=29.7-0.02475x.
$$

Solving ${P}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 29.7-0.02475x & =0 \\ x & =1\,200\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $x=1\,200$ lies in the interval $0<x<2\,000.$ All that's left now is to confirm that $x=1\,200$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:   

$$
{P}^{″}(x)=-0.02475<0.
$$

Since the second derivative is negative, the point $x=1\,200$ is indeed a  maximum of $P(x).$ 

Our candidates are $x=0,$ $x=1\,200,$ and $x=2\,000.$ Computing $P(x)$ at each of these values, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0) & =-1\,000 \\ P(1\,200) & =-1\,000+29.7(1\,200)-0.012375(1\,200)^{2}=16\,820\,✓ \\ P(2\,000) & =-1\,000+29.7(2\,000)-0.012375(2\,000)^{2}=9\,500\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the factory will have a maximum annual profit when it produces $1\,200$ units per year."] ["question-a7b5b31e-6d04-57eb-9051-cd4496c07c09" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-b3b3f22b-6d4c-5cc5-9130-cf5e72b4c48c" :answer-field/id #uuid "b3b3f22b-6d4c-5cc5-9130-cf5e72b4c48c"] ["answer-5dedbf55-c0ea-588a-a30e-090c0bd91a10" :answer/id #uuid "5dedbf55-c0ea-588a-a30e-090c0bd91a10"] ["answer-5dedbf55-c0ea-588a-a30e-090c0bd91a10" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-5dedbf55-c0ea-588a-a30e-090c0bd91a10" :answer/value "1200"] ["answer-field-b3b3f22b-6d4c-5cc5-9130-cf5e72b4c48c" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-b3b3f22b-6d4c-5cc5-9130-cf5e72b4c48c" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-b3b3f22b-6d4c-5cc5-9130-cf5e72b4c48c" :answer-field/correct "answer-5dedbf55-c0ea-588a-a30e-090c0bd91a10"] ["answer-field-b3b3f22b-6d4c-5cc5-9130-cf5e72b4c48c" :answer-field/choices "answer-5dedbf55-c0ea-588a-a30e-090c0bd91a10"] ["question-a7b5b31e-6d04-57eb-9051-cd4496c07c09" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-b3b3f22b-6d4c-5cc5-9130-cf5e72b4c48c"] [17592186101019 :knowledge-point/questions "question-a7b5b31e-6d04-57eb-9051-cd4496c07c09"] ["question-2888ed58-7e1b-57a5-91ea-2124b7fe040e" :question/id #uuid "2888ed58-7e1b-57a5-91ea-2124b7fe040e"] ["question-2888ed58-7e1b-57a5-91ea-2124b7fe040e" :question/math-academy-id "q-18671"] ["question-2888ed58-7e1b-57a5-91ea-2124b7fe040e" :question/problem "A hotel has $71$ rooms. The manager has observed that when the room rate is $$50$ per night, all rooms are occupied and, for every $$2$ increase in the rate, a single room is vacated. If the maintenance per rented room is $$4$ per night, what rate per room should the manager set to obtain the maximum profit?"] ["question-2888ed58-7e1b-57a5-91ea-2124b7fe040e" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

First, note that if there are $x$ *vacant* rooms, the hotel has $(71-x)$ occupied rooms, and the rate per room is $(50+2x)$ dollars. So, the total revenue (in dollars) is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & ={{(71-x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{occupied rooms}}\times \,\,\,{{(50+2x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{rate per room}} \\  & =3\,550+142x-50x-2{x}^{2} \\  & =3\,550+92x-2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, for having $(71-x)$ rooms rented out, the hotel has a cost (in dollars) of 

$$
\begin{aligned}C(x) & =4(71-x) \\  & =284-4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the profit function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\ P(x) & =3\,550+92x-2{x}^{2}-(284-4x) \\  & =3\,266+96x-2{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We note that the permitted domain is $0\le x\le 71.$ 

We need to find the critical points of $P(x)$ for $0<x<71$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=96-4x,
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 96-4x & =0 \\ 4x & =96 \\ x & =24\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $x=24$ lies in the interval $0<x<71.$ All that's left now is to confirm that $x=24$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:

$$
{P}^{″}(x)=-4<0
$$

Since the second derivative is negative, the point $x=24$ is indeed a local maximum of $P(x).$ And since $P(x)$ is quadratic, we conclude that $x=24$ is a global maximum of $P(x).$ 

Therefore, we conclude that the hotel will have a maximum profit level when there are $x=24$ vacant rooms. 

We know that the rate per room is $(50+2x)$ dollars. If there are $24$ vacant rooms, then the rate per room is

$$
\begin{aligned}50+2(24) & =$98.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the manager should charge a room rate of $$98$ per night."] ["question-2888ed58-7e1b-57a5-91ea-2124b7fe040e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["question-8babed00-8ea0-55fe-9919-358ba07b0746" :question/math-academy-id "q-119098"] ["question-8babed00-8ea0-55fe-9919-358ba07b0746" :question/problem "A coffee shop can produce up to $500$ cups of coffee per day. When the price per cup of coffee is $$3,$ the coffee shop sells all of them, and, for each dollar increase in the price, $50$ cups remain unsold. If the cost for producing a cup of coffee is $$0.40,$ what price per cup should be set to obtain the maximum profit?"] ["question-8babed00-8ea0-55fe-9919-358ba07b0746" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

First, note that if there are $x$ hundreds of *unsold* cups of coffee, the coffee shop sells $(5-x)$ hundreds of cups of coffee, and the price per cup is $(3+2x)$ dollars. So, the total revenue (in hundreds of dollars) is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & ={{(5-x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{sold cups of coffee}}\times \,\,\,{{(3+2x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{price per cup}} \\  & =15+10x-3x-2{x}^{2} \\  & =15+7x-2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, for selling $(5-x)$ hundreds of cups of coffee, the coffee shop has a cost (in hundreds of dollars) of 

$$
\begin{aligned}C(x) & =0.4(5-x) \\  & =2-0.4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the profit function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\ P(x) & =(15+7x-2{x}^{2})-(2-0.4x) \\  & =13+7.4x-2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We note that the permitted domain is $0\le x\le 5.$ 

We need to find the critical points of $P(x)$ for $0<x<5.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=7.4-4x,
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 7.4-4x & =0 \\ 4x & =7.4 \\ x & =1.85\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $x=1.85$ lies in the interval $0<x<5.$ All that's left now is to confirm that $x=1.85$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:

$$
{P}^{″}(x)=-4<0
$$

Since the second derivative is negative, the point $x=1.85$ is indeed a local maximum of $P(x).$ And since $P(x)$ is quadratic, we conclude that $x=1.85$ is a global maximum of $P(x).$ 

Therefore, we conclude that the coffee shop will have a maximum profit level when there are $185$ unsold cups of coffee.  

We know that the price per cup is $(3+2x)$ dollars. If there are $1.85$ hundreds of unsold cups of coffee, then the price per cup is

$$
\begin{aligned}3+2(1.85) & =$6.7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coffee shop should sell each cup of coffee for $$6.7.$"] ["question-8babed00-8ea0-55fe-9919-358ba07b0746" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\  & =15x-(700+2x) \\  & =13x-700.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Let's find out how."] [17592186101994 :tutorial/content "Recall that the price function $p(x)$ gives the *price per unit* at which a company sells $x$ units of a good. 

The revenue function $R(x)$ associated with a price function $p(x)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & =(\text{number of units})\cdot (\text{price per unit}) \\  & =x\cdot p(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Also, recall that the cost function $C(x)$ associated with producing $x$ units of a good can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C(x) & =(\text{fixed cost})+(\text{number of units})\cdot (\text{cost per unit}) \\  & =(\text{fixed cost})+x\cdot (\text{cost per unit})\end{aligned}
$$

The quantity $x\cdot (\textrm{cost per unit})$ is sometimes called the **variable cost** since it is the part of the cost function $C(x)$ that is dependent on the number of units $x$ produced by the company. 

Finally, if we know the revenue function $R(x)$ and the cost function $C(x),$ then the profit function $P(x)$ is given by

$$
P(x) = R(x) - C(x).
$$"] [17592186101902 :step/math-academy-id 644177] [17592186101903 :step/math-academy-id 644178] [17592186101904 :step/math-academy-id 644181] [17592186101905 :step/math-academy-id 644182] $$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1\end{aligned}]+(-2)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1\end{aligned}]+(-2)\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1\end{aligned}]+(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((3)\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}10 & -10 \\ -10 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-524b5d0d-afb1-56e2-9f18-7dc1697e2495" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b4cd93bf-3a8c-5f18-b352-8eff8b26fc90" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-4d6df4b5-e301-58fd-845a-847c7a249d39" :question/worked-solution "The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{13}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =7-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(-x)) \\  & =7-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3x) \\  & =7-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)=f(x),$ we have that $f$ is even.

For the Fourier series on $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the sine coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Here, $f(x)$ is even and $\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)$ is odd, so $f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)$ is odd.

Now, the integral of an odd function over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$ is $0.$ Thus, ${b}_{n}=0$ for all $n\ge 1.$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ is $\text{even}$ and the $\text{sine terms}$ in its Fourier series must be zero."] ["question-8c279eae-dd78-5b67-912d-9a38a48eda28" :question/difficulty customers per month."] ["question-61246f8d-17fc-5cf4-84dc-d3e84d220ded" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that June $1$st corresponds to $t=1.$

We use the forward difference approximation formula

$$
{q}^{′}(t)≈\frac{q(t+h)-q(t)}{h}
$$

at the point $t=1.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible. In this case, we choose $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}^{′}(1) & ≈\frac{q(1+1)-q(1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{q(2)-q(1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{120-59}{1} \\  & =61.\end{aligned}
$$

So, using a forward difference approximation, the rate of change in the number of customers on June $1$st is approximately $61$ customers per month."] ["question-61246f8d-17fc-5cf4-84dc-d3e84d220ded" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-cf8bd0d4-e2df-5b96-ba24-b2e56674f0f8" :answer-field/id #uuid "cf8bd0d4-e2df-5b96-ba24-b2e56674f0f8"] ["answer-876c3c8e-19f9-56b2-a451-3c2578ba7af7" :answer/id #uuid "876c3c8e-19f9-56b2-a451-3c2578ba7af7"] ["answer-876c3c8e-19f9-56b2-a451-3c2578ba7af7" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-876c3c8e-19f9-56b2-a451-3c2578ba7af7" :answer/value "61"] ["answer-field-cf8bd0d4-e2df-5b96-ba24-b2e56674f0f8" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-cf8bd0d4-e2df-5b96-ba24-b2e56674f0f8" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-cf8bd0d4-e2df-5b96-ba24-b2e56674f0f8" :answer-field/correct "answer-876c3c8e-19f9-56b2-a451-3c2578ba7af7"] ["answer-field-cf8bd0d4-e2df-5b96-ba24-b2e56674f0f8" :answer-field/choices "answer-876c3c8e-19f9-56b2-a451-3c2578ba7af7"] ["question-61246f8d-17fc-5cf4-84dc-d3e84d220ded" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-cf8bd0d4-e2df-5b96-ba24-b2e56674f0f8"] [17592186092388 :knowledge-point/questions "question-61246f8d-17fc-5cf4-84dc-d3e84d220ded"] ["question-7a6777e5-075d-540c-87f4-265fdb022242" :question/id #uuid "7a6777e5-075d-540c-87f4-265fdb022242"] ["question-7a6777e5-075d-540c-87f4-265fdb022242" :question/math-academy-id "q-166363"] ["question-7a6777e5-075d-540c-87f4-265fdb022242" :question/problem "From the given data, the best backward difference approximation for the rate at which the number of customers was changing on June $1$st is{{field-1}}
customers per month."] ["question-7a6777e5-075d-540c-87f4-265fdb022242" :question/worked-solution "Again, we use the fact that June $1$st corresponds to $t=1.$

We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{q}^{′}(t)≈\frac{q(t)-q(t-h)}{h}
$$

at the point $t=1.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible. In this case, we choose $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}^{′}(1) & ≈\frac{q(1)-q(1-1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{q(1)-q(0)}{1} \\  & =\frac{59-0}{1} \\  & =59.\end{aligned}
$$

So, using a backward difference approximation, the rate of change in the number of customers on June $1$st is approximately $59$ customers per month."] ["question-7a6777e5-075d-540c-87f4-265fdb022242" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-74caf0bf-cacd-5f28-aa72-d801b776ea5f" :answer-field/id #uuid "74caf0bf-cacd-5f28-aa72-d801b776ea5f"] ["answer-9593a22e-5aa8-5e2e-b0d9-870be17ad1c0" :answer/id #uuid "9593a22e-5aa8-5e2e-b0d9-870be17ad1c0"] ["answer-9593a22e-5aa8-5e2e-b0d9-870be17ad1c0" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-9593a22e-5aa8-5e2e-b0d9-870be17ad1c0" :answer/value "59"] ["answer-field-74caf0bf-cacd-5f28-aa72-d801b776ea5f" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-74caf0bf-cacd-5f28-aa72-d801b776ea5f" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-74caf0bf-cacd-5f28-aa72-d801b776ea5f" :answer-field/correct "answer-9593a22e-5aa8-5e2e-b0d9-870be17ad1c0"] ["answer-field-74caf0bf-cacd-5f28-aa72-d801b776ea5f" :answer-field/choices "answer-9593a22e-5aa8-5e2e-b0d9-870be17ad1c0"] ["question-7a6777e5-075d-540c-87f4-265fdb022242" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-74caf0bf-cacd-5f28-aa72-d801b776ea5f"] [17592186092391 :knowledge-point/questions "question-7a6777e5-075d-540c-87f4-265fdb022242"] ["question-ae9e49ed-eef5-5e75-8ccc-b6af327fb845" :question/id #uuid "ae9e49ed-eef5-5e75-8ccc-b6af327fb845"] ["question-ae9e49ed-eef5-5e75-8ccc-b6af327fb845" :question/math-academy-id "q-166364"] ["question-ae9e49ed-eef5-5e75-8ccc-b6af327fb845" :question/problem "Using a trapezoidal sum with two equal subintervals, ${\int }_{0}^{4}q(t)\,\text{d}t≈${{field-1}}
."] ["question-ae9e49ed-eef5-5e75-8ccc-b6af327fb845" :question/worked-solution "The general formula for the trapezoidal rule states that

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}q(t)\,\text{d}t≈\frac{1}{2}[q(a)+2(q({t}_{1})+q({t}_{2})+…+q({t}_{n-1}))+q(b)]Δt,
$$

where $n$ is the number of trapezoids and $Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}$ is the step size.

Here, we have the following values:

* The number of trapezoids is $n=2.$

* The corresponding interval is $[0,4],$ so we have $a=0$ and $b=4.$

* The step size is given by

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{4-0}{2}=2.
$$

Using the above values, the general formula becomes

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}q(t)\,\text{d}t≈\frac{1}{2}[q(0)+2q(2)+q(4)]\cdot 2.
$$

Substituting the appropriate numbers into the above expression gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}q(t)\,\text{d}t & ≈\frac{1}{2}[0+2(120)+108]\cdot 2 \\  & =240+108 \\  & =348.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ae9e49ed-eef5-5e75-8ccc-b6af327fb845" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-dff10b37-1425-5f08-9969-ac5f0106b371" :answer-field/id #uuid "dff10b37-1425-5f08-9969-ac5f0106b371"] ["answer-32acdae7-2eaa-5d7b-bea5-1d4a19711cdc" :answer/id #uuid "32acdae7-2eaa-5d7b-bea5-1d4a19711cdc"] ["answer-32acdae7-2eaa-5d7b-bea5-1d4a19711cdc" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-32acdae7-2eaa-5d7b-bea5-1d4a19711cdc" :answer/value "348"] ["answer-field-dff10b37-1425-5f08-9969-ac5f0106b371" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-dff10b37-1425-5f08-9969-ac5f0106b371" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-dff10b37-1425-5f08-9969-ac5f0106b371" :answer-field/correct "answer-32acdae7-2eaa-5d7b-bea5-1d4a19711cdc"] ["answer-field-dff10b37-1425-5f08-9969-ac5f0106b371" :answer-field/choices "answer-32acdae7-2eaa-5d7b-bea5-1d4a19711cdc"] ["question-ae9e49ed-eef5-5e75-8ccc-b6af327fb845" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-dff10b37-1425-5f08-9969-ac5f0106b371"] [17592186092181 :knowledge-point/questions "question-ae9e49ed-eef5-5e75-8ccc-b6af327fb845"] ["question-6b1c7ad5-e07c-5b25-9e08-a2e2aa0ac237" :question/id #uuid "6b1c7ad5-e07c-5b25-9e08-a2e2aa0ac237"] ["question-6b1c7ad5-e07c-5b25-9e08-a2e2aa0ac237" :question/math-academy-id "q-166365"] ["question-6b1c7ad5-e07c-5b25-9e08-a2e2aa0ac237" :question/problem "Use your answer to part 3 to approximate the average number of customers at the campsite during the first $4$ months.

."] ["question-6b1c7ad5-e07c-5b25-9e08-a2e2aa0ac237" :question/worked-solution "The average value of a continuous function $q(t)$ on a closed interval $[a,b]$ is given by

$$
{q}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}q(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}q(t)\,\text{d}t & ≈348.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{q}_{\text{ave}}≈\frac{348}{4-0}=87.
$$"] ["question-6b1c7ad5-e07c-5b25-9e08-a2e2aa0ac237" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-5847b751-f98d-563e-aaf4-cc2c04b1208d" :answer-field/id #uuid "5847b751-f98d-563e-aaf4-cc2c04b1208d"] ["answer-a73ce7dc-ebea-528a-9250-92701e8d78cb" :answer/id #uuid "a73ce7dc-ebea-528a-9250-92701e8d78cb"] ["answer-a73ce7dc-ebea-528a-9250-92701e8d78cb" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-a73ce7dc-ebea-528a-9250-92701e8d78cb" :answer/value "87"] ["answer-field-5847b751-f98d-563e-aaf4-cc2c04b1208d" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-5847b751-f98d-563e-aaf4-cc2c04b1208d" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-5847b751-f98d-563e-aaf4-cc2c04b1208d" :answer-field/correct "answer-a73ce7dc-ebea-528a-9250-92701e8d78cb"] ["answer-field-5847b751-f98d-563e-aaf4-cc2c04b1208d" :answer-field/choices "answer-a73ce7dc-ebea-528a-9250-92701e8d78cb"] ["question-6b1c7ad5-e07c-5b25-9e08-a2e2aa0ac237" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-5847b751-f98d-563e-aaf4-cc2c04b1208d"] [17592186064267 :knowledge-point/questions "question-6b1c7ad5-e07c-5b25-9e08-a2e2aa0ac237"] ["question-9de46d9e-0321-5243-8082-f7e3f4b58ad3" :question/id #uuid "9de46d9e-0321-5243-8082-f7e3f4b58ad3"] ["question-9de46d9e-0321-5243-8082-f7e3f4b58ad3" :question/math-academy-id "q-166366"] ["question-9de46d9e-0321-5243-8082-f7e3f4b58ad3" :question/problem "For $0\le t\le 8,$ the equation ${q}^{′}(t)=0$ has at least{{field-1}}

probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|x/2|}}{4},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/2}}{2},\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$"] [17592186134541 :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/2}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/2}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186134541 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-b905210f-a059-572c-8e25-2b36e139ca53" :answer/id #uuid "b905210f-a059-572c-8e25-2b36e139ca53"] }_{i=1}^{3}{\sum }_{j=1}^{2}({i}^{2}-{j}^{2})=$"] ["question-62a31be5-1f88-5fce-bc3d-c7a604a6e638" :question/worked-solution "First, we write out the inner summation by summing over the index $j:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sum }_{j=1}^{2}({i}^{2}-{j}^{2}) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{3}[{\sum }_{j=1}^{2}({i}^{2}-{j}^{2})] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{3}(({i}^{2}-{1}^{2})+({i}^{2}-{2}^{2})) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{3}(({i}^{2}-1)+({i}^{2}-4)) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{3}(2{i}^{2}-5)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we sum over the index $i:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}(2{i}^{2}-5) & =(2(1)^{2}-5)+(2(2)^{2}-5)+(2(3)^{2}-5) \\  & =-3+3+13 \\  & =13\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-62a31be5-1f88-5fce-bc3d-c7a604a6e638" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-cb74bb6d-eb9e-5168-b33b-f718103e0618" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-62a31be5-1f88-5fce-bc3d-c7a604a6e638"] ["question-6d3ae80f-587f-5674-9679-5efb33bf0d2c" :question/id #uuid "6d3ae80f-587f-5674-9679-5efb33bf0d2c"] ["question-6d3ae80f-587f-5674-9679-5efb33bf0d2c" :question/math-academy-id "q-157227"] ["question-6d3ae80f-587f-5674-9679-5efb33bf0d2c" :question/problem "Consider the following vectors:

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $-3{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+2{a}_{3}=0.$

II. ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$

III. The set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent."] ["question-6d3ae80f-587f-5674-9679-5efb33bf0d2c" :question/worked-solution "We say that three vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}=0
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

With that in mind, let's look at each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+2{a}_{3} & =-3[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12+0+2 \\ 3+6+4 \\ 0+0+10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 13 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. The equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ corresponds to the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 5{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we can reorder the equations in this system as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ 5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system using back substitution, we find that the solution is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-6d3ae80f-587f-5674-9679-5efb33bf0d2c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] Find $(u+9v)\cdot w+v\cdot (u+7w).$"] [17592186134208 :question/worked-solution "Since $v$ and $w$ are orthogonal vectors, we have that $v\cdot w=0.$ Therefore, using linearity of the dot product to expand the parentheses, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(u+9v)\cdot w+v\cdot (u+7w) & =u\cdot w+(9v)\cdot w+v\cdot u+v\cdot (7w) \\  & =u\cdot w+9(v\cdot w)+v\cdot u+7(v\cdot w) \\  & =u\cdot w+9\cdot 0+v\cdot u+7\cdot 0 \\  & =u\cdot w+v\cdot u \\  & =(4\cdot 2+(-2)\cdot (-5)+1\cdot 7+(-3)\cdot (-3)) \\  & +((-4)\cdot 4+3\cdot (-2)+5\cdot 1+4\cdot (-3)) \\  & =(8+10+7+9)+(-16-6+5-12) \\  & =34-29 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186134208 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186131287 :answer-field/correct 17592186131292] ["question-a905591c-e962-54f6-a8cc-c6c8bf83d953" :question/id #uuid "a905591c-e962-54f6-a8cc-c6c8bf83d953"] ["question-a905591c-e962-54f6-a8cc-c6c8bf83d953" :question/math-academy-id "q-39987"] ["question-a905591c-e962-54f6-a8cc-c6c8bf83d953" :question/problem "If $u=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 2k \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ and $v=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1 \\ 4 \\ k\end{aligned}]$ are orthogonal vectors, then $k=$"] ["question-a905591c-e962-54f6-a8cc-c6c8bf83d953" :question/worked-solution "Since $u⊥v$, they are orthogonal vectors, we have that their dot product is equal to zero.
First, let's calculate the dot product in terms of $k$:

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot v & ={u}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}+{u}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}+{u}_{3}\cdot {v}_{3}+{u}_{4}\cdot {v}_{4} \\  & =1\cdot (-5)+(-3)\cdot 1+2k\cdot 4+(-2)\cdot k \\  & =-5-3+8k-2k \\  & =6k-8\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the dot product to zero, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6k-8 & =0 \\ 6k & =8 \\ k & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a905591c-e962-54f6-a8cc-c6c8bf83d953" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-3235cbb9-445e-59a3-8203-e82d292f2f8e" :answer-field/id #uuid $a-b?$"] ["question-308fc3e8-c583-59b4-999d-1160fdbc5784" :question/worked-solution "Given that $u$ is orthogonal to $v$ and $w$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}u\cdot v=0 \\ u\cdot w=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's consider the first equation $u\cdot v=0.$ Calculating the dot product in terms of $a$ and $b$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot v & =0 \\ a\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 4+b\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 5 & =0 \\ 2a-4-2b+10 & =0 \\ 2a-2b & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, for the second equation $u\cdot w=0$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot w & =0 \\ a\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot (-3)+b\cdot 1+2\cdot (-3) & =0 \\ a+3+b-6 & =0 \\ a+b & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the values of $a$ and $b$, we need to solve the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2a-2b=-6 \\ a+b=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the second equation by $-2$ and adding the result to the first equation, we obtain

$$
-4b=-12\,⟹\,b=3.
$$

Substituting $b=3$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2a-2(3) & =-6 \\ 2a-6 & =-6 \\ 2a & =0 \\ a & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have that

$$
a-b=0-3=-3.
$$"] ["question-308fc3e8-c583-59b4-999d-1160fdbc5784" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-c7504c88-811b-566a-be94-9e43fa618465" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot v & ={u}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}+{u}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}+{u}_{3}\cdot {v}_{3}+{u}_{4}\cdot {v}_{4} \\  & =7\cdot 3+k\cdot (-k-1)+k\cdot (-7)+3\cdot (-12) \\  & =21-{k}^{2}-k-7k-36 \\  & =-{k}^{2}-8k-15 \\  & =-({k}^{2}+8k+15)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the dot product to zero, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-({k}^{2}+8k+15) & =0 \\ -(k+5)(k+3) & =0 \\ k & =-5,-3.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-fff3565b-721f-5145-afe3-b8fe4b216b1a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-721d2419-eef5-5e91-a81c-c762d04fdf6d" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}{2}^{kx} \\  & ={2}^{2k}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{15}{x+3} \\  & =\frac{15}{2+3} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}(2x+k) \\  & =2(2)+k \\  & =4+k.\end{aligned}
$$

We also note that $f(2)=4+k.$ 

So, for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) \\ 4+k & =3 \\ k & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function is continuous at $x=2$ for the value $k=-1.$"] ["question-74f22eb1-bd58-519a-94ee-cc4da7917518" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-9629635b-88c4-533d-9081-d8a1cc525da1" :answer-field/id #uuid "9629635b-88c4-533d-9081-d8a1cc525da1"] ["answer-60a7f976-f4de-5958-8041-40d291b11ea0" :answer/id #uuid "60a7f976-f4de-5958-8041-40d291b11ea0"] ["answer-60a7f976-f4de-5958-8041-40d291b11ea0" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-60a7f976-f4de-5958-8041-40d291b11ea0" :answer/value "-1"] ["answer-field-9629635b-88c4-533d-9081-d8a1cc525da1" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-9629635b-88c4-533d-9081-d8a1cc525da1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-9629635b-88c4-533d-9081-d8a1cc525da1" :answer-field/correct "answer-60a7f976-f4de-5958-8041-40d291b11ea0"] ["answer-field-9629635b-88c4-533d-9081-d8a1cc525da1" :answer-field/choices "answer-60a7f976-f4de-5958-8041-40d291b11ea0"] ["question-74f22eb1-bd58-519a-94ee-cc4da7917518" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-9629635b-88c4-533d-9081-d8a1cc525da1"] [17592186100804 :knowledge-point/questions "question-74f22eb1-bd58-519a-94ee-cc4da7917518"] [17592186101995 :tutorial/content "Consider the function $f(x)$ below:
![](images/cb/cbdbe44a94ff036c74957691e30ed3652d50d2a8dbaa50b29827408f242492bb.svg)

The function $f(x)$ seems to have a point discontinuity at $x=1.$ However, by selecting a particular value for $k,$ we can remove the point discontinuity and make the function continuous.

We can find this value of $k$ by forcing the limit of the function to be equal to the value of the function at $x=1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to 1} f(x) = f(1)
$$

Remember that $\lim\limits_{x\to 1} f(x)$ represents the value that $f(x)$ approaches as $x$ gets closer and closer, but not equal, to $1.$ So, when evaluating $\lim\limits_{x\to 1} f(x),$ we need to use the function definition for $x \neq 1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{{x}^{2}+x-2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{(x-1)(x+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\cancel{(x-1)}(x+1)}{\cancel{(x-1)}(x+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{x+1}{x+2} \\  & =\frac{1+1}{1+2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=1,$ the function is defined as $f(x)=k.$ So, $f(1)=k$, and for continuity we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}f(x) & =f(1) \\ \frac{2}{3} & =k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to make $f(x)$ continuous at $x=1,$ we need to choose $k=\dfrac{2}{3}.$"] [17592186101077 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0] ["question-dcb73b7c-8cd5-5969-93ed-1bf898ab0795" :question/id #uuid "dcb73b7c-8cd5-5969-93ed-1bf898ab0795"] ["question-dcb73b7c-8cd5-5969-93ed-1bf898ab0795" :question/math-academy-id "q-140491"] ["question-dcb73b7c-8cd5-5969-93ed-1bf898ab0795" :question/problem "Consider the **orthonormal** set $U$ below. $$"] ["question-dcb73b7c-8cd5-5969-93ed-1bf898ab0795" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2}.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{3}$, we need to find a third vector $x$ such that $‖x‖=1,$ and

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}{x}_{1}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{17}}{x}_{2}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}{x}_{3}=0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{17}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{17}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\sqrt{17}\cdot {R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=\sqrt{2}\cdot {R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=\frac{4}{3}{x}_{3},$ and from the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{4}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=3,$ we obtain the vector 
$x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ 

Now, we need to normalize $x.$ Notice that $‖x‖=\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}}=\sqrt{34}.$ So, we normalize $x$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{‖x‖}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{34}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{3}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{34}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|+|{x}_{3}|=|\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}|+|\frac{4}{\sqrt{34}}|+|\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}|=\frac{10}{\sqrt{34}}.$"] ["question-dcb73b7c-8cd5-5969-93ed-1bf898ab0795" :question/difficulty "step-e74678fc-cdaa-5c80-82f2-06de36ea9535"] [17592186199502 :tutorial/content "It's possible to derive Taylor polynomials for functions of more than two variables. However, increasing the number of variables significantly increases the number of terms in the Taylor polynomial. 

Ideally, we'd like a compact expression for the quadratic Taylor polynomial that works for all twice-differentiable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.$ This can be achieved using matrix notation. 

To see how, let's consider the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f(x,y)$ about $(a,b){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote ![](images/6f/6fe1832d2f4ae2b36446386e5d0ec7c41f898f4e575af9238695c37f7c427250.svg) and ![](images/49/496eacb98651e3fab4c0d0a7b44ab283fadad1c07243da485aeb0c4a059d5712.svg) then the total derivative of $f(x,y)=f(\mathbf{x})$ at $(a,b)=\mathbf{a}$ is given by

![](images/d6/d696700e295d9f43111ac53602b936a991b7766af654cedaa5afdae21b088a59.svg)

With that in mind, we can rewrite the linear part of the approximation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Linear approximation} & =f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b) \\  & =f(a)+[\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-a \\ y-b\end{aligned}] \\  & =f(a)+[\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]) \\  & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is just our usual linear approximation of a function $f.$

The second derivative of $f$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is given by

![](images/de/de2a75a6681e1e393b21b60de9d7aeee748a8e6d04010ab713b40f0f41f239cf.svg)

Therefore, using the fact that $f_{xy} = f_{yx},$ we can rewrite the quadratic part of the approximation using matrix multiplication as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Quadratic part} & =\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}x-a & y-b\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-a \\ y-b\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}([\begin{aligned}x & y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a & b\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our quadratic Taylor polynomial can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)}}+{{\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this formula is more compact and has clear similarity with the corresponding formula for functions with one variable:

$$
f(x) \approx  \overbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{Quadratic part}}
$$"] [17592186100581 :question/problem "![](images/3e/3e9a879522107eb2b2381a688d1173fdf6a93a8b81686fd2f21c815008ec35df.png)

Let's understand how this process works by studying a specific example.

The graph of $y = f'(x),$ the *derivative* of $f(x),$ is shown in the picture below. 

![](images/1e/1ef0f93de1825106880b3fdcd3c704c72e0748df277e5098064d6ee9abc9bdf8.png)

The areas of the shaded regions are indicated on the diagram. Additionally, it is known that $f(-2)=3.$ Our goal is find the *maximum* value of $f(x)$ on the interval $x\in [-2,2].$

To find the maximum value of $f(x),$ we use the candidates test.

According to the candidates test, the maximum value of $f(x)$ on $[-2,2]$ must occur at a critical point or an endpoint of the interval. Therefore, we proceed as follows.

**Step 1**: Find the critical points:

We see that $f'(x)$ is defined everywhere on $x\in (-2,2),$ so there are no non-stationary critical points. Additionally, we see that $f'(x)=0$ at $x=-1.$ Therefore, the candidates are 

$$
x=-2,\quad x=-1,\quad x=2.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the value of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus:

- The value of $f(x)$ at the left endpoint is given:

$$
f(-2) = 3
$$

- To compute $f(-1),$ we apply the fundamental theorem of calculus. Since the area of the left triangle in our picture equals ${\color{red}{1}},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1) & =f(-2)+{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3+1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

- To compute $f(2),$ we apply the fundamental theorem of calculus once more. Using the fact that the area of the left triangle equals ${\color{red}{1}}$ and the area of the right triangle equals ${\color{blue}{\dfrac32}},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & =f(-2)+{\int }_{-2}^{2}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3+1-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we *subtracted* the area of the right triangle since it lies *under* the $x$-axis.

**Step 3**: Select the largest value of $f$ from our candidates. 

Comparing the values of $f$ found in step $2,$ we have

$$
f_{\text{max}} = \max\left\lbrace 3, 4, \dfrac{5}{2} \right\rbrace = 4.
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is $f_{\text{max}}=4,$ and the value of $x$ that maximizes $f(x)$ is $x_\text{max}=-1.$"] [17592186101079 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0] ["question-8118b4f8-280b-5e14-bfe6-ca499d29c282" :question/id #uuid "8118b4f8-280b-5e14-bfe6-ca499d29c282"] ["question-8118b4f8-280b-5e14-bfe6-ca499d29c282" :question/math-academy-id "q-68052"] ["question-8118b4f8-280b-5e14-bfe6-ca499d29c282" :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4x-5},$ which of the following statements is correct?

I. ${lim}_{x\to (-5)^{+}}f(x)=+\infty $

II. ${lim}_{x\to (-5)^{-}}f(x)=+\infty $

III. ${lim}_{x\to (-5)}f(x)=-\infty $"] ["question-8118b4f8-280b-5e14-bfe6-ca499d29c282" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4x-5} \\  & =\frac{x}{(x-1)(x+5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function $f(x)=\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4x-5}$ has two vertical asymptotes $x=1$ and $x=-5.$

To compute the one-sided limits as $x\to (-5),$ we evaluate $f(x)$ at $x$-values very close to $x=-5$ from the right and from the left.

| $x$ | $-5.1$ | $-5.01$ | $-5$ | $-4.99$ | $-4.9$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $-8.36$ | $-83.36$ | $\text{undefined}$ | $83.30$ | $8.30$ |

All values are negative and get smaller and smaller as $x\to (-5)$ from the left and all values are positive and get larger and larger as $x\to (-5)$ from the right. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-5)^{-}}f(x)=-\infty ,\,\,\,{lim}_{x\to (-5)^{+}}f(x)=+\infty .

$$

:question/problem "Given that $f(x)=\frac{x}{6+x-{x}^{2}},$ which of the following statements is correct?

I. ${lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}f(x)=-\infty $

II. ${lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}f(x)=-\infty $

III. ${lim}_{x\to (-2)}f(x)=\text{DNE}$"] ["question-f73e65ac-e638-502e-b806-c6b1908dab88" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x}{6+x-{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{x}{(x-3)(x+2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

This implies that the function $f(x)=\frac{x}{6+x-{x}^{2}}$ has two vertical asymptotes $x=-2$ and $x=3.$

To compute the one-sided limits as $x\to (-2),$ we evaluate $f(x)$ at $x$-values very close to $x=-2$ from the right and from the left.

| $x$ | $-2.01$ | $-2.001$ | $-2$ | $-1.999$ | $-1.99$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $≈40.12$ | $≈400.12$ | $\text{undefined}$ | $≈-399.88$ | $≈-39.88$ |

All values are positive and get larger and larger as $x\to (-2)$ from the left and all values are negative and get smaller and smaller as $x\to (-2)$ from the right. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}f(x)=+\infty ,\,\,\,{lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}f(x)=-\infty .
$$

Consequently, statement I is false and II is true.

Finally, since both left and right-sided limits at $x=-2$ are different, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-2)}f(x)=\text{DNE},
$$

and therefore III is also true.

In conclusion, only statements II and III are true. A plot of the function is shown below.

:question/problem "Given that $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}+4x}{{x}^{2}+3x-4},$ which of the following statements is correct?

I. ${lim}_{x\to (-4)^{-}}f(x)=\infty $

II. ${lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x)=-\infty $

III. ${lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x)=-\infty $"] ["question-0bc0c5f8-ceb7-5dd9-9846-93db9391162e" :question/worked-solution "First, let's factor the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}+4x}{{x}^{2}+3x-4} \\  & =\frac{x(x+4)}{(x+4)(x-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is  $x\ne -4,1,$ and we notice that the function can be simplified:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=\frac{x}{x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we see that the function has the only vertical asymptote $x=1.$ So statement I is false.

To find  ${lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x),$ and  ${lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x),$ we evaluate $f(x)$ at $x$-values very close to $x=1$ from the left and right.

| $x$ | $0.99$ | $0.999$ | $1$ | $1.001$ | $1.01$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $-99$ | $-999$ | $\text{undefined}$ | $1\,001$ | $101$ |

All values are negative and get smaller and smaller as $x\to 1$ from the left and all values are positive and get larger and larger as $x\to 1$ from the right. Therefore, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x)=-\infty ,\,{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x)=\infty 
$$

Consequently, statement II is false and statement III is true.

\theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$"] ["question-b688c283-ffe1-5279-a25b-e224f4238243" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{2}{e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{(\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2{e}^{2\theta }+2{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2{e}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{e}^{\theta }{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2({e}^{\pi /2}-{e}^{\pi /4}) \\  & =2{e}^{\pi /4}({e}^{\pi /4}-1)\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b688c283-ffe1-5279-a25b-e224f4238243" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-c2bc4d54-53d7-5960-8596-76e1189178c5" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-acde0039-9e1f-5668-bb5b-a5df57c98611" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta })^{2}+{(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )^{2}+{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,\theta {|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =\sqrt{2}\text{ }(\pi -\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\frac{1}{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\frac{1}{{\theta }^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{\theta })}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{\theta }^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{1}{{\theta }^{2}}+\frac{1}{{\theta }^{4}}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{{\theta }^{2}+1}{{\theta }^{4}}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\pi }\frac{\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}+1}}{{\theta }^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-4cb23656-32ad-5111-abf0-812956e034d5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2ddef5b4-7fd6-526e-90d2-54235e050d54" :answer-field/id #uuid Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and   

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented. 

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=i\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & =-{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-1}^{1}t\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t-0 \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{t}{2}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[\frac{\pi }{4}-0]-[-\frac{\pi }{4}-0] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-053eddb0-5c93-560e-b92c-a89951cbd49c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-cdfd2c93-cc42-5e18-b039-6099f904aa29" :answer-field/id #uuid \begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-fdacb1ae-ddf6-5106-9485-7c1e14bd18a9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a2eb735b-b5bd-5b47-b78f-f9e6cc0794cf" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-6ae04e3b-017d-534f-b76c-ac600584e435" :question/math-academy-id "q-126568"] ["question-6ae04e3b-017d-534f-b76c-ac600584e435" :question/problem "Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the functions $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)?$

I. $P(x,y)=-y-\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$

II. $P(x,y)=x$ and $Q(x,y)=y$

III. $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=6{y}^{2}$"] ["question-6ae04e3b-017d-534f-b76c-ac600584e435" :question/worked-solution "According to Green's theorem, if 

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Pair I gives the required area. In this case,
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1+\operatorname{sin}⁡y$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

- Pair II does *not* give the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0\ne 1.
$$

- Pair III gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""] ["question-6ae04e3b-017d-534f-b76c-ac600584e435" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i+12\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,dx & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\cdot (-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡2t(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-18{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =18{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =6({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ad2198cd-84ab-52d9-a653-128de0924655" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-0b42e264-51ff-5675-8ac9-a399601959a2" :answer-field/id #uuid - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-6I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-1I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $V:$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$"] ["question-79df1f11-1c43-51b8-8e99-4f8efb003972" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c4360e51-0f64-590c-bba8-917045fffada" :answer-field/id #uuid **Step 2**: Compute the values of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus:

The function is made up of one triangle and one trapezoid. Let's add the areas bounded by these shapes to our diagram:

![](images/d8/d811c4920b4ddb05170afc1f0c38fe216c23139556b6f7e10829b663e894a7fb.png)

$$

**Step 3**:  Select the smallest value of $f$ from our candidates.

$$
{f}_{\text{min}}=min\{1.5,1,4\}=1.
